title: Being Right
overview: This week investigates why the inner Judge can keep talking even after you recognize its criticism. Gary proposes that superiority supplies a small emotional reward: the character gets to feel correct, worthy, or acceptable while declaring somebody else wrong. The assignment is to notice that reward in detail, including when the criticism is directed at yourself. This builds on the earlier character inventories and observer practice. It does not ask you to abandon accurate thinking, practical standards, or useful feedback. The distinction is between a clear assessment of what works and a comparison used to manufacture a superior identity. Earlier practices offer other ways to experience appreciation and acceptance.
outcomes: Identify a specific judgment and the superior identity it creates.
Trace the feeling the Judge gets from being correct, including during self-criticism.
Replace a complaint with a clear assessment or another way of connecting.

concepts.title: The reward behind the criticism
concepts.explanation: A judgment may look like an opinion about a bridge, a meal, a driver, or your own performance. Gary asks you to look one layer deeper: what does making that opinion mean about the speaker? The Judge may construct an image of being smarter, more capable, or more deserving of respect. In the course's framework, that self-image provides a feeling of acceptance or worth. The task is not to decide in advance that every opinion hides superiority. Observe a real episode and find out whether this emotional payoff is actually present for you.

concepts.title: Two positions inside self-criticism
concepts.explanation: Feeling terrible after a mistake can obscure another position in the same inner conversation. One character says that you failed; another agrees and feels small. The Judge, however, may feel knowledgeable and justified while delivering the criticism. Gary calls these the Judge and Victim positions. Writing them separately can expose the contrast between their emotions. This is a way to describe patterns of thought, not a diagnosis or a claim that you have separate people inside you. Notice both voices without turning the observation into another accusation against yourself.

concepts.title: Assessment without a hierarchy of worth
concepts.explanation: The lesson explicitly preserves clear assessment. You can recognize that a car is unreliable, an arrangement is ineffective, or a decision needs correction without deciding that someone is inferior. Ask what happened, what consequence matters, and what action would help. The extra step of ranking a person's worth is not necessary to solve the practical problem. This distinction matters because giving up contempt can otherwise sound like giving up discernment. The course's aim is to reduce the emotional investment in superiority while keeping the ability to make useful decisions.

concepts.title: Keep the good feeling; examine the route
concepts.explanation: The obstacles sheet anticipates resistance: if being right produces a good feeling, relinquishing it can seem like relinquishing happiness. Gary's response is to revisit gratitude, acceptance, silent mind, and meditation as alternative routes. Complaining can also serve as social glue, so changing the pattern may require a new way of talking with others. You might still discuss a real difficulty while leaving out the ranking of people. The practical question becomes how to preserve connection and self-respect without needing someone else to be wrong or beneath you.

concepts.title: A belief is more than a sentence
concepts.explanation: The supporting explanation of belief change separates surface thoughts, underlying beliefs, emotions, conviction, and identity. A statement such as needing to be right may cover a fear of being stupid or rejected. Replacing the sentence alone may leave the surrounding emotional and identity structure intact. The course therefore asks for detailed observation from a neutral viewpoint rather than a quick positive slogan. Treat this as Gary's model for investigation: record what you can actually notice, and leave a possible hidden belief as a hypothesis until your own examples support it.

visual.title: The Judge's reward loop
visual.intro: A study illustration of the course framework, to compare with a real example rather than assume it fits.

steps.label: Notice a flaw
steps.detail: Something or someone does not meet an expectation.

steps.label: Compare identities
steps.detail: The Judge implies that it knows better.

steps.label: Feel a reward
steps.detail: Correctness becomes a route to worth, pride, or acceptance.

steps.label: Repeat the criticism
steps.detail: The small payoff helps keep the pattern going.

visual.takeaway: Interrupt the loop by observing the payoff and finding another way to express acceptance.

practice.title: Inventory what the Judge is right about
practice.cadence: Listen to the lesson and write about judgments as you notice them. The written assignment gives no fixed number of minutes or daily quota.

steps.title: Choose one recent comment
steps.body: Write a specific criticism or complaint in the words used by the Judge. Begin with a manageable example such as a minor inconvenience, an opinion about a service, or a small mistake.

steps.title: Write the comparison
steps.body: Describe what the Judge claims to know better and what it says about the other person or about the criticized version of you. Keep each character's viewpoint separate.

steps.title: Follow the feeling
steps.body: Notice any pride, relief, correctness, self-acceptance, or superiority in the judging position. Also record other feelings, including discomfort; do not invent a pleasurable reward if you cannot find one.

steps.title: Name the construction
steps.body: Write how the story and self-image appear to produce that emotion. Is the Judge picturing itself as smarter, more disciplined, or more deserving? Use the observer perspective rather than endorsing the ranking.

steps.title: Try another route
steps.body: Revisit a familiar gratitude, acceptance, or quiet-attention practice. Explore whether the valued feeling can be experienced without the comparison. This is experimentation, not a demand to make yourself feel better immediately.

steps.title: Keep useful information
steps.body: Finish with a clear assessment of the situation and any practical action. Notice the difference between describing a problem and assigning somebody a lower personal worth.

prompts: What exact sentence did the Judge say?
What image of itself did that sentence support?
What did each side of the inner conversation feel?
What useful assessment remains if I remove the superiority?

obstacles.title: I only notice feeling bad
obstacles.response: The questions sheet suggests separating the judging position from the position receiving the criticism. The Judge's reward can be subtle; investigate without forcing a conclusion.

obstacles.title: Complaining is how we connect
obstacles.response: The obstacles sheet acknowledges this social habit. Look for another form of connection: interest, humor, shared activity, or a discussion of the practical issue without contempt.

obstacles.title: Now I judge myself for judging
obstacles.response: That may be another turn of the same pattern. Return to the assignment's curiosity and acceptance: describe what the character does before trying to fix it.

stories.title: The ugly bridge
stories.summary: Gary describes driving with a friend who criticized a bridge's architecture, despite not being an architect or engineer. He uses the comment to examine two subjects at once. On the surface, the friend is discussing the bridge. Underneath, the implied story is that he has better judgment or taste than the people who designed it. In Gary's interpretation, that comparison builds a flattering self-image and a small feeling of being right. The lesson is not that the bridge must actually be beautiful, nor that only experts can have opinions. It is that the emotional reward of a criticism can be different from its literal subject.
stories.lesson: Ask what a criticism does for the speaker's self-image, as well as whether its factual content is useful.

stories.title: The winner and the Judge afterward
stories.summary: A businessman in Gary's account repeatedly returned to gambling despite wanting to stop. Through an inventory, he associated the image of winning with a powerful feeling of success and self-love. Gary then points to a second pattern after gambling: the Judge condemns the behavior while feeling that it knows better, and the criticized position feels ashamed. The story illustrates Gary's emotional-reward interpretation of this person's experience. It is not presented here as a general explanation of addiction or a treatment plan. Its relevance to this week is the surprising possibility that self-criticism can carry a rewarding sense of correctness alongside obvious distress.
stories.lesson: The feeling a behavior promises may differ from the object it appears to pursue.

storiesNote: These are paraphrases of Gary's accounts, not independently verified case histories.

cheatsheet.principle: Notice the emotional payoff of superiority without surrendering clear judgment about practical matters.
remember: The surface topic may hide a self-image comparison.
The Judge and the criticized position can feel different emotions.
Correctness can become a condition for self-acceptance.
Assessment asks what works; contempt ranks a person's worth.
Gratitude and acceptance offer other routes to good feelings.
cheatsheet.try: Turn one complaint into a factual observation and a useful next action.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Making the discovery of superiority into a new reason to condemn yourself.
cheatsheet.question: What feeling would I lose if I stopped needing to be right here?

quiz.question: What does the weekly assignment ask you to investigate behind being right?
options: Whether other people should agree with you
The emotional reward and self-image attached to correctness
How to stop making all practical assessments
quiz.explanation: The focus is the Judge's emotional payoff, not the abandonment of useful discernment.

quiz.question: Which response best fits clear assessment?
options: This arrangement is unreliable; I need a workable alternative.
Only an idiot would arrange it this way.
I am superior because I spotted the problem.
quiz.explanation: The first statement identifies function and action without ranking personal worth.

quiz.question: What if superiority is hard to notice during self-criticism?
options: Invent a positive feeling so the model fits
Conclude that the exercise has failed
Separate the Judge's viewpoint from the viewpoint receiving the criticism
quiz.explanation: The questions sheet recommends observing the two character positions and their different emotions.

reflection: Which judgment was easiest to observe without believing it?
What changed when I separated assessment from superiority?
How might I connect with someone this week without a shared complaint?

title: Entitlement
overview: Entitlement examines the gap between actively creating a life and believing that life owes you a particular outcome. Gary asks you to inventory attachments, ownership language, and imagined agreements about what should remain in your life. The aim is to appreciate and engage with people and circumstances while recognizing uncertainty. This can be a challenging lesson because it touches loss, change, and mortality. The practice guide also explicitly encourages self-respect and says not to allow mistreatment. Its philosophical discussion of entitlement is not a removal of practical rights, responsibilities, or needs. Supporting articles add an essential balance: you can acknowledge needs, ask clearly, negotiate, and respect another person's choice.
outcomes: Distinguish a chosen intention from an expectation treated as a guarantee.
Identify one attachment and the imagined agreement behind it.
Make a clear request while preserving both self-respect and another person's choice.

concepts.title: Intention and expectation do different jobs
concepts.explanation: In the lesson, intention directs participation: make a plan, learn skills, take action, and influence what you can. Expectation becomes problematic when a desired picture is treated as something reality must deliver. A business owner can improve a service but cannot guarantee that customers will choose it. A person can value a relationship without controlling its future. Gary is asking you to notice the added demand, not to stop caring. In your inventory, separate the action you choose from the outcome you cannot fully command and observe the emotional difference.

concepts.title: The vocabulary of attachment
concepts.explanation: The assignment highlights words such as my, mine, own, owed, deserve, and have. These words are clues, not automatic evidence of a problem. Writing my home is ordinary language; the useful question is what hidden promise accompanies it. Does the mind assume permanence, obedience, fairness, or immunity from loss? Gary describes these imagined promises through the Princess archetype and the disappointed Victim response. Put the supposed agreement on paper so you can examine it. Ask who actually made it, what is observable, and what is a wish or interpretation.

concepts.title: Temporary does not mean unimportant
concepts.explanation: The common questions frame possessions, relationships, and the body as temporarily available rather than permanently guaranteed. Gary connects this recognition with deeper gratitude: familiarity can make something precious seem ordinary or owed. The practice is not to predict catastrophe or rehearse loss until you become afraid. It is to notice what is here now and how you wish to use the time available. Grief and difficult feelings need not be judged as proof that you are doing the course badly. The inquiry concerns assumptions added to experience, not a compulsory emotional response.

concepts.title: Needs are different from demands
concepts.explanation: The supporting article Getting Your Needs Met Without Being Needy rejects the idea that you should need nobody. It describes connection, support, creativity, rest, and meaningful participation as important parts of a satisfying life. The companion on asking for what you want recommends clear requests, explaining why they matter, appreciation, and negotiation. Another person can decline, and you can choose what relationship or arrangement works for you. Releasing a claim that one particular person must satisfy a need does not mean denying the need or accepting an arrangement that consistently neglects it.

concepts.title: Respect survives the inquiry
concepts.explanation: The practice guide explicitly says to treat yourself well, respect yourself, and not let others mistreat you. Hold that instruction alongside the lesson's provocative discussion of fairness and entitlement. You can examine an interpretation while still taking practical protective action, asking for repair, or changing a relationship. The course language is a framework for personal reflection, not a legal conclusion about what someone owes you. A useful distinction is between insisting that the world could never change and deciding how you will respond to the world as it actually is.

visual.title: Two ways to hold a desired outcome
visual.intro: A study illustration of Gary's distinction between engaged intention and a guaranteed-outcome story.

steps.label: I value this
steps.detail: Name the relationship, object, experience, or opportunity that matters.

steps.label: I can influence this
steps.detail: Choose the request, preparation, or action within your reach.

steps.label: I cannot guarantee this
steps.detail: Recognize other people's choices and changing circumstances.

steps.label: I can appreciate this
steps.detail: Meet what is present with care while remaining able to adapt.

visual.takeaway: Appreciation and purposeful action can coexist with uncertainty.

practice.title: Write an inventory of attachments
practice.cadence: Listen to the Entitlement lesson, more than once if useful, and write about attachments. The written assignment specifies no fixed session length or daily quota.

steps.title: Choose an ordinary starting point
steps.body: Begin with an attachment that feels manageable: a plan going smoothly, a possession working, or somebody responding as expected. You do not need to begin with a major loss.

steps.title: Write what feels yours or owed
steps.body: Record the exact expectation. Notice words such as mine, deserve, owed, should, or always, and describe what you expect the person or circumstance to do.

steps.title: Trace the consequence
steps.body: Write what happens emotionally when the expectation is not met, or what you imagine would happen. Distinguish the actual event from the story of what it means.

steps.title: Find the imagined agreement
steps.body: Ask where the guarantee came from. Was it a real mutual agreement, a hope, a childhood promise to yourself, or an assumption? Preserve the difference between real commitments and total control over outcomes.

steps.title: Separate intention from control
steps.body: Write what you still want to create and one action you can take. Then name the part that depends on other people, time, or circumstances.

steps.title: Practice appreciation and respect
steps.body: Notice something valuable that is present now. If a need is unmet, make a clear request or decide on a boundary rather than treating detachment as a reason to disregard yourself.

prompts: What do I feel is mine, owed, or guaranteed?
What do I actually control, influence, or neither?
What wish has become an unspoken contract?
What request or action respects both me and the other person?

obstacles.title: This sounds like giving up
obstacles.response: The lesson repeatedly distinguishes disengagement from acting without a guarantee. Keep the plan and the effort; examine the demand that the result must match your picture.

obstacles.title: The inquiry feels too large
obstacles.response: Use a smaller everyday example. The course acknowledges strong emotional protest when comforting assumptions are questioned; you do not need to force a sweeping realization.

obstacles.title: Having a need feels weak
obstacles.response: The supporting articles explicitly validate needs and interdependence. Practice asking and negotiating rather than suppressing the desire or demanding that one person fulfill it.

stories.title: The bookstore across the street
stories.summary: Gary imagines a person who has built a beloved small bookstore. A large chain opens across the street, draws customers away, and the original business closes. The owner may experience this as a stolen dream. Gary changes the viewpoint: customers have choices, the competitor has its own aims, and the owner can influence service or selection without controlling those outside decisions. He uses the example to distinguish a cherished project from a guaranteed result. It is a philosophical illustration of expectation, not a claim that all business practices are fair or that a disappointed owner should feel nothing.
stories.lesson: Care for a project and improve what you can without treating success as a promise reality has made.

stories.title: A blank sheet on the refrigerator
stories.summary: The lesson proposes writing on a sheet of paper everything you assume will be in your life tomorrow or next week. Gary then offers a contrasting picture: leave the sheet blank as a symbol that none of those experiences is absolutely guaranteed. A planned family visit can still be booked and enjoyed; the blank sheet does not cancel the ticket or the intention. It changes the mental posture from assuming the visit is owed to appreciating that it happens. The image is meant to make a usually invisible layer of expectation easier to notice.
stories.lesson: Planning is useful; taking the result for granted is an additional mental step.

storiesNote: The bookstore is an illustrative scenario. The blank sheet is an exercise/metaphor offered in the lesson.

cheatsheet.principle: Keep intention, action, and self-respect while loosening the demand for a guaranteed outcome.
remember: Ownership words can reveal hidden assumptions.
Influence is different from control.
A valued relationship is not a permanent possession.
Having needs is compatible with respecting another person's choice.
Detachment is not indifference or permission for mistreatment.
Gratitude notices what familiarity has made invisible.
cheatsheet.try: Write: I want __; I can act by __; I cannot guarantee __.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Using the lesson to shame grief, deny a need, or abandon a practical boundary.
cheatsheet.question: Can I remain engaged without demanding that this turn out exactly as imagined?

quiz.question: Which statement best captures the lesson's distinction?
options: If I cannot control a result, I should stop trying.
I can act toward a result without treating it as guaranteed.
Appreciation requires having no needs.
quiz.explanation: Gary keeps intention and action while questioning the extra demand for certainty.

quiz.question: What do the supporting articles recommend when you need something from another person?
options: Ask clearly, explain its importance, and allow negotiation or refusal.
Hide the need so you will not look weak.
Make the person responsible for your entire emotional state.
quiz.explanation: Needs and requests are legitimate; the articles distinguish them from coercive demands.

quiz.question: What is a useful first response to the word mine in an inventory?
options: Give the object away immediately.
Decide that all ownership is wrong.
Investigate the unspoken expectation accompanying the word.
quiz.explanation: The words are clues to an assumption, not automatic instructions about possessions.

reflection: Which expectation did I discover only after an event disappointed me?
What did I appreciate more when I stopped treating it as guaranteed?
Where do I need a clearer request or boundary?

title: Viewpoint
overview: Viewpoint develops the ability to move beyond a familiar interpretation of another person. The two guided recordings invite you to imagine the lives of your mother and father, or the people who raised you, from inside their circumstances rather than only from your childhood position. The written practice then extends this approach to other relationships. The exercise is an exploration of imagination and possible context, not a way to recover facts or certify someone's motives. Gary explicitly says there is no required outcome and offers writing as an alternative to visualization. The obstacles sheet permits setting the assignment aside when childhood trauma or violence makes it emotionally too much.
outcomes: Distinguish what you know about another person's life from what you are imagining.
Explore how family, culture, resources, and available choices may shape a viewpoint.
Use perspective-taking to question certainty while preserving your own experience and boundaries.

concepts.title: A viewpoint includes a whole background
concepts.explanation: The recordings do not begin with a parent's behavior toward you. They begin around that person's birth: their parents, the household economy, education, religion, social expectations, siblings, and available choices. This wider frame helps interrupt the assumption that another person's actions were entirely about you. The practice is to imagine what living inside those constraints might have felt like. It does not establish that a particular constraint explains a particular action. Keep known history separate from possibilities, and let a genuine question remain unanswered when information is missing.

concepts.title: Imagination can loosen certainty without proving a story
concepts.explanation: Gary explains that the exercise may be useful even if the imagined viewpoint is not the other person's actual experience. Trying on and taking off a different interpretation can reveal that your usual interpretation is not the only conceivable one. This is the core skill, rather than guessing correctly or arriving at a predetermined feeling. A vivid image is still an image, and a newly compelling story is still a hypothesis. Where appropriate, a later conversation with the person or someone who knew them can add information, but the exercise itself is not evidence.

concepts.title: Compassion and factual acknowledgment can coexist
concepts.explanation: The supporting video begins by acknowledging that a parent or relative may have made real mistakes. It then asks how comparison with an imagined ideal parent influences the present judgment. The inquiry can reveal a hidden list of what the person should have known or become. This does not require denying harmful events, approving them, or resuming contact. The useful distinction is between understanding possible influences and excusing conduct. You can recognize somebody's limitations and retain your own account of what happened, the effect it had, and what you need now.

concepts.title: Writing is a valid route into perspective
concepts.explanation: Some people visualize easily; others work better through language. The practice guide explicitly offers writing about a parent's life from that person's viewpoint. You can describe what a day might have involved, what choices appeared available, and what social consequences might have followed. Gary also suggests fiction as a way to exercise this capacity. The aim is not a polished story or a convincing performance. It is a more flexible relationship to your own assumptions. Label imagined details as imagined so the writing remains exploratory rather than turning into a new authoritative history.

concepts.title: Readiness matters more than completion
concepts.explanation: The obstacles sheet recounts a client who had deferred this assignment for a year and says that putting it aside can be appropriate when the material is emotionally too much. It suggests reconsidering later rather than forcing the exercise. The questions also permit using adoptive parents, grandparents, or whoever actually raised you. Another person with a less charged history can be a place to explore the broader skill. No dramatic insight, reconciliation, or feeling of compassion is required to mark an honest practice attempt; noticing a limit is also useful information.

visual.title: From one story to several possible lenses
visual.intro: A study illustration of the course's perspective-taking method; the possibilities are hypotheses, not recovered facts.

steps.label: My familiar account
steps.detail: Name the event and the meaning you usually give it.

steps.label: Their wider context
steps.detail: Consider time, place, upbringing, resources, and pressures.

steps.label: Possible inner experience
steps.detail: Imagine a viewpoint while labeling unknown details.

steps.label: A more open question
steps.detail: Notice what you would now want to understand or ask.

visual.takeaway: A useful result can be less certainty, not a replacement story you must believe.

practice.title: Dream or write another viewpoint
practice.cadence: The assignment asks you to follow both guided recordings and permits repeating them. The Mother introduction suggests being comfortably still for 20–30 minutes; the Father recording is shorter. There is no requirement to achieve a particular result or finish an emotionally overwhelming session.

steps.title: Choose the person and your readiness
steps.body: Use a mother, father, or another person who raised you. If this history is too charged, the course permits deferring it; you can explore the general skill with another person instead.

steps.title: Settle in a quiet place
steps.body: Follow the recording while seated safely and free to pause. Gary specifically says not to do the closed-eye guided practice while driving. Bring attention to breathing and allow familiar judgments to rest for the moment.

steps.title: Begin before your own childhood
steps.body: Imagine the time and place of the person's birth. Consider their parents, siblings, household resources, education, religious context, and social expectations. Note what is known and what is an imagined possibility.

steps.title: Move through choices and constraints
steps.body: Imagine growing up with those influences, seeking education or work, making relationship choices, and eventually caring for children. Ask what seemed possible from within that life rather than only from your current viewpoint.

steps.title: Write what you noticed
steps.body: Use writing if visualization is difficult. Record a change in interpretation, an unanswered question, or no particular change. Avoid treating imagined scenes as historical evidence.

steps.title: Extend with care
steps.body: If useful, try the same approach with a partner, colleague, or service worker. A respectful question may be more useful than another assumption. No contact, forgiveness, or reconciliation is required by this study activity.

prompts: What do I know about this person's early life, and what remains unknown?
What opportunities or pressures might I be overlooking?
How does the event look through one possible alternative lens?
What changed in my certainty, and what boundaries still matter?

obstacles.title: I cannot visualize
obstacles.response: The practice guide explicitly recommends writing the person's life from their viewpoint as another route. Use concrete details and mark uncertainty.

obstacles.title: I feel overwhelmed by family history
obstacles.response: The obstacles sheet says to put the exercise aside if it is emotionally too much, including where there was trauma or violence. You can stop, choose another subject, or revisit later.

obstacles.title: I need to know whether my imagined version is true
obstacles.response: The Mother recording says not to assume you truly entered the person's viewpoint. The immediate goal is flexibility of perspective, not factual certainty.

stories.title: A tollbooth attendant's day
stories.summary: Gary describes a friend's daughter who was assigned in high school to write about someone else's life. She chose a tollbooth attendant and wrote about standing beside the highway amid passing traffic and exhaust fumes. Her description was detailed enough for a reader to imagine being there. Gary uses this as a bridge: entering another person's visible surroundings is one step; imagining their inner pressures, choices, and concerns is another. The anecdote supports writing as a practical alternative to a guided visualization. It does not claim that the student knew the actual thoughts of any particular attendant.
stories.lesson: Concrete circumstances can open a door to perspective, while the inner life still requires humility about what you do not know.

stories.title: A house of cards built on early interpretations
stories.summary: In the Mother recording, Gary compares childhood interpretations to cards on the first level of a house of cards. Later beliefs and choices may rest on those early assumptions. Considering an event through another viewpoint can therefore affect more than that single memory: other conclusions may become less convincing too. The metaphor describes a possible change in a belief structure. It does not require every childhood interpretation to be wrong or predict that a dramatic collapse will occur. Some people report little surprise, some discover unanswered questions, and some choose not to undertake the exercise at that time.
stories.lesson: Questioning an early assumption can have wider effects, but there is no required breakthrough.

storiesNote: The tollbooth account is Gary's anecdote. The house of cards is his metaphor for connected beliefs.

remember: Start with the person's background, not only their behavior toward you.
Known history and imagined context are different.
Writing is an approved alternative to visualization.
Understanding does not require approval, contact, or reconciliation.
There is no required insight or emotional outcome.
The course explicitly permits deferring an overwhelming exercise.

cheatsheet.watchFor: Replacing one certainty about a person with another invented certainty.
cheatsheet.question: What might I not know about the life behind this behavior?

A hypothesis that may broaden perspective
Proof of what the parent intended
quiz.explanation: The guided introduction explicitly avoids assuming that the imagined viewpoint is true.

quiz.explanation: The obstacles sheet allows deferral, including where childhood trauma or violence makes the exercise overwhelming.

title: Image of Perfection
overview: A criticism often announces that you fell short without revealing the standard it used. This week makes that hidden standard explicit. Gary asks you to begin with one small judgment, interview the Judge about exactly what would have satisfied it, and examine the resulting criteria for reasonableness. The exercise extends the earlier work on characters and being right by investigating the platform underneath the critical voice. It preserves goals and useful learning while questioning the use of those goals as conditions for worth. The written guide strongly cautions against making an overwhelming master list at the beginning: investigate one judgment at a time from a skeptical, observing position.
outcomes: Translate a vague criticism into a specific hidden expectation.
Test a standard against time, learning, real constraints, and its treatment of other people.
Keep a useful goal while removing the demand that it determine your worth.

concepts.title: The criticism is only the visible edge
concepts.explanation: A sentence such as I should not have done that can appear persuasive because the outcome was undesirable. Gary asks what complete picture sits behind it: what should you have done, known, become, or achieved, and by when? The Judge may imply foresight, instant learning, universal approval, or an impossible combination of accomplishments. Writing those criteria turns an indistinct feeling of failure into something examinable. The aim is not to prove that every decision was wise. It is to distinguish practical information from the unspoken requirement that you should already have been an idealized person.

concepts.title: Detail reveals the actual rule
concepts.explanation: General answers such as be successful or be good enough can leave the rule intact. The lesson recommends following up: how successful, in which field, by what age, with what resources, and what would finally satisfy the voice? A deadline is often part of the image of perfection. Ask what learning and experience would have been necessary to meet it at that earlier time. Some standards become less credible as soon as they are fully described. Others require further examination. Record the rule accurately rather than replacing it immediately with a reassuring statement.

concepts.title: Try the standard on someone you love
concepts.explanation: One test in the lesson is to apply the criterion to another person, then to people in general. Would you withhold love from a child for struggling at mathematics? Would you expect every novice to display an expert's discipline immediately? This changes the viewpoint from being the accused person to examining a rule. The point is not to recruit other people into criticism. It is a private thought experiment about consistency and reasonableness. If the standard still seems credible, look again at the concrete details and at whether you are observing it or feeling trapped inside it.

concepts.title: A goal is not a verdict on your worth
concepts.explanation: The obstacles sheet explicitly distinguishes goals from images of perfection. A goal can direct action toward a useful future. The Judge uses an ideal image to condemn you for not having arrived already, sometimes attaching an invented deadline from years ago. You can keep the desired skill, relationship, or financial objective while changing the commentary surrounding it. Gary points to enjoyment, inspiration, appreciation of quality, satisfaction, and the desire for a better life as other sources of motivation. The assignment dismantles a punitive comparison, not every aspiration or standard of workmanship.

concepts.title: One judgment is enough for a session
concepts.explanation: The supporting article includes a graduate student's extensive list of perfection demands, but the practice guide tells learners not to begin by copying that scale. A huge list can become another inventory of supposed deficiencies if you believe it. Start with one issue and enough detail to see its structure. Only later, when skepticism is established, might combining standards reveal contradictions. The method depends on the observer position developed earlier in the course. If you feel overwhelmed or increasingly condemned, reduce the scope and return to the earlier practices instead of pushing for a bigger list.

visual.title: From verdict to inspectable criteria
visual.intro: A study illustration of the course's interview method for the Image of Perfection.

steps.label: Hear the verdict
steps.detail: Write one exact should or not-good-enough statement.

steps.label: Interview the Judge
steps.detail: Ask what would have counted as completely satisfactory.

steps.label: Expose the criteria
steps.detail: Name the accomplishment, knowledge, deadline, and contradictions.

steps.label: Test the rule
steps.detail: Check its reasonableness and whether you would apply it to others.

steps.label: Keep useful direction
steps.detail: Choose a goal or learning step without the condemnation.

visual.takeaway: The hidden standard can be questioned more effectively once it is specific.

practice.title: Investigate one image of perfection
practice.cadence: Listen to the lesson, repeating if useful. Work on one small judgment at a time; the practice guide does not prescribe a fixed session length or number of entries.

steps.title: Select one small judgment
steps.body: Write the exact critical statement, ideally about a manageable issue. Do not start by compiling every expectation you have about your entire life.

steps.title: Ask what should have happened
steps.body: Interview the Judge: what action, result, quality, or accomplishment would have made this acceptable? Write the answer as the character's rule rather than an established truth.

steps.title: Follow the details
steps.body: Ask how much, how often, by when, and under what circumstances. What knowledge, discipline, resources, or other people's behavior would have been necessary? Keep questioning until the standard is concrete.

steps.title: Check reasonableness
steps.body: Look for impossible foresight, incompatible requirements, or an unrealistic learning timetable. Would you expect this from someone with the same experience and circumstances?

steps.title: Apply the comparison test
steps.body: Imagine applying the same standard and withholding the same acceptance from someone you love, then from people generally. Notice whether the rule still seems sensible.

steps.title: Separate learning from condemnation
steps.body: Keep any useful lesson or chosen goal. Write one constructive action that follows from the facts, alongside the perfection demand you no longer need to accept.

prompts: What exact judgment am I investigating?
What would have completely satisfied the Judge, and by when?
What would someone have needed in order to meet that demand?
Would I apply this rule to a person I love?
What useful goal remains without the verdict on my worth?

obstacles.title: Without the Judge I will lose motivation
obstacles.response: The obstacles sheet says to retain goals while questioning punitive standards. Explore motivation through interest, love of the activity, quality, satisfaction, or the wish for a better life.

obstacles.title: The standard still feels true
obstacles.response: The questions sheet asks whether you are looking as a skeptic or from the criticized character's position. Return to one concrete criterion and test it rather than arguing with a global feeling.

obstacles.title: The list is overwhelming
obstacles.response: The practice guide expressly says not to make a comprehensive list at first. Work with one small judgment, and revisit observer or acceptance practice if the exercise becomes self-condemning.

stories.title: What would make Bill good enough?
stories.summary: Gary recounts a client he calls Bill who thought a woman he admired should be with someone more worthy. Asked what would make him good enough, Bill's imagined requirements became increasingly specific: extraordinary wealth, a record-setting mountain climb, a professional baseball career with repeated All-Star selections, exceptional philanthropy, and a presidency judged the best ever. Some criteria contradicted others, such as retaining immense wealth while giving it away. Seeing the complete standard helped Bill question the voice using it. The lesson's account is not a checklist to imitate; the written assignment specifically recommends investigating one small judgment at a time.
stories.lesson: Vague inadequacy can rest on criteria that become implausible once fully exposed.

stories.title: The athlete and her daughter's grades
stories.summary: A workshop participant who had competed on an Olympic team still felt inadequate because she had struggled academically, including with mathematics as a child. In Gary's account, she had tied being lovable to meeting a standard of academic ability. He asked whether she would withhold love from her daughter if the child struggled at school. She immediately rejected that rule for her daughter. Applying the same criterion outside herself opened a possibility that it need not govern her own worth either. The shift came through testing the rule, not by proving she was actually the best student.
stories.lesson: A standard can lose authority when you see how you would treat somebody else under it.

storiesNote: Both stories are paraphrases of the teacher's accounts. They illustrate the inquiry rather than promise the same result for every learner.

cheatsheet.principle: Question the detailed standard behind the judgment, while keeping useful goals and learning.
remember: A criticism often conceals its criteria.
Ask what would finally satisfy the Judge.
Include the deadline and the learning required.
Check for contradictions and impossible foresight.
Try the rule on someone you love.
Begin with one small judgment, not a life-sized perfection list.
cheatsheet.try: Complete: To be acceptable, the Judge says I should have __ by __.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Turning the inventory into a new list of things you must achieve to deserve acceptance.
cheatsheet.question: Is this a chosen direction for my life, or a standard being used to punish me?

quiz.question: What is the recommended initial scope of the assignment?
options: Every imperfection you can identify in your life
One small judgment investigated in detail
Only the judgments that are obviously false
quiz.explanation: The written guide warns that a comprehensive list can overwhelm the learner and reinforce self-judgment.

quiz.question: Which distinction does the obstacles sheet emphasize?
options: Goals guide action; an image of perfection is used to condemn you for falling short.
Any goal is necessarily an image of perfection.
Giving up self-criticism means giving up effort.
quiz.explanation: The lesson preserves goals and other forms of motivation while questioning punitive comparisons.

quiz.question: Why apply the standard to another person?
options: To persuade them to criticize you more
To prove they are worse than you
To step outside your own agreement and examine whether the rule is reasonable
quiz.explanation: The comparison is a perspective shift for examining the standard, not an exercise in judging others.

reflection: What hidden deadline or impossible requirement did I find?
Which test made the standard easier to see clearly?
What goal do I still choose, and how can I pursue it with less self-condemnation?
coverageNote: The study guide covers the assignment, lesson, obstacles, questions, perfection inventory article, and video about the Judge's claimed motivational purpose. The full week includes The feeling of not being good enough audio for further exploration. The graduate student's long inventory is an example, not the recommended starting assignment.

title: Emotional Mastery
overview: This week shifts from analyzing beliefs to practicing a different relationship with emotions. Gary asks you to intentionally create a feeling, experience it, detach from the supporting image or story, and return toward neutral. Pleasant emotions come first; the written questions explicitly say to skip unpleasant emotions if you cannot detach easily or if thoughts and images become uncontrolled. The larger aim is freedom to feel, rather than using positivity to suppress what is already present. The lesson builds on attention, acceptance, and releasing emotions. It describes mastery as a long practice, not a one-week achievement or a score you should meet.
outcomes: Practice generating a manageable feeling and returning attention to present sensations.
Distinguish deliberate emotional practice from suppressing an existing emotion.
Recognize when to rest, reduce intensity, or skip an unpleasant-emotion exercise.

concepts.title: A change in relationship, not a ban on reactions
concepts.explanation: Gary describes a move from experiencing emotions only as something that happens to you toward noticing some capacity to shape, feel, and release them. In the exercise, memories, images, posture, breath, or direct attention can help generate an emotion. Observing this process can make the feeling seem less mysterious. The course's language of being a creator is an invitation to practice, not proof that every emotion is instantly voluntary. Record the degree of influence you actually experience. Difficulty with a feeling is information about the practice, not a failure of character.

concepts.title: Detaching is as important as creating
concepts.explanation: The exercise is incomplete if you only intensify a feeling. The second half is to release the image, story, or memory used to evoke it, relax tension, and return attention to breathing and the body's present sensations. Earlier acceptance practice supplies part of this skill. Gary's desired result is a less fearful relationship with feeling, so that emotions can be experienced without automatically acting out the accompanying story. The questions sheet makes the practical boundary clear: if an unpleasant feeling does not release readily, stop that part and stay with pleasant, manageable emotions for now.

concepts.title: Do not turn gratitude into a lid
concepts.explanation: The practice guide warns against switching on gratitude simply to cover an unpleasant emotion. That can become another way to avoid feeling what is present. This distinction connects the current week to the earlier releasing-emotions work: developing confidence with feeling is meant to support fuller acceptance, not constant replacement of sadness or anger with an approved mood. Before beginning, notice whether you are choosing a practice session or trying to escape a feeling already asking for attention. The study goal is a broader range of comfortable contact with emotions, not a permanently cheerful performance.

concepts.title: Fear of a feeling can shape a decision
concepts.explanation: The lesson gives examples of avoiding a request because of anticipated embarrassment, or over-helping because saying no might bring guilt. Gary argues that these anticipated emotions can quietly control choices even after the verbal logic is understood. Becoming more comfortable with a manageable feeling may create room for a different action. This does not mean ignoring genuine interpersonal risks or forcing exposure to overwhelming emotion. Keep the practical situation and the imagined emotional consequence separate. The exercise concerns your relationship with feeling; it does not guarantee a safe response from another person.

concepts.title: Rest and scale are part of practice
concepts.explanation: The obstacles sheet anticipates fatigue after only one or a few repetitions and tells you to rest. The questions recommend smaller emotions and gradual increases only when comfortable. Gary estimates that the dramatic speed he calls mastery could take months or years, and immediately emphasizes that the greater benefit is being able to remain present with feelings. Treat those timelines as his teaching description rather than a forecast for you. A short, manageable attempt with a clear return to neutral can be more appropriate than a long session aimed at proving intensity or endurance.

visual.title: The create-and-release cycle
visual.intro: A study illustration of the course exercise, using a manageable scale and the stopping guidance from the written questions.

steps.label: Choose
steps.detail: Select a pleasant feeling you are comfortable exploring.

steps.label: Evoke
steps.detail: Use an image, memory, or attention to invite the feeling.

steps.label: Notice
steps.detail: Observe sensations without needing to act on a story.

steps.label: Release
steps.detail: Let the image go and relax toward neutral.

steps.label: Rest and review
steps.detail: Check your state before deciding whether to repeat.

visual.takeaway: The ability to stop and return matters more than intensity or speed.

practice.title: Create, feel, and dissolve a manageable emotion
practice.cadence: The lesson suggests practicing periodically through the day, including brief repetitions, and the obstacles sheet requires rest when tired. It gives no daily quota. Mastery is described as a long-term development, not a result required this week.

steps.title: Begin safely and check your state
steps.body: Choose a quiet, stationary setting where attention can stay with the exercise. Notice what you already feel. If you are trying to cover a difficult existing emotion, return to the earlier acceptance or releasing practice instead.

steps.title: Start with a pleasant feeling
steps.body: Choose gratitude, affection, joy, or another comfortable emotion. Use a memory or imagined situation if helpful. Follow the questions sheet's advice to begin at a manageable scale rather than chasing the largest possible intensity.

steps.title: Observe the experience
steps.body: Notice bodily sensations, breathing, facial expression, posture, and any image or story supporting the feeling. Stay curious about what is actually happening.

steps.title: Let the supporting material go
steps.body: Release the imagined scene or memory, soften muscular tension, and bring attention back to breathing and present bodily sensations. Give yourself time to return toward neutral.

steps.title: Decide whether to repeat
steps.body: Rest if tired. Only consider an unpleasant emotion if the process is comfortable and detaching is easy. The course explicitly says to skip that part if you get stuck or if the thought and image sequence runs uncontrolled.

steps.title: Write the change in relationship
steps.body: Record what you could evoke, what helped you release, and what limits you noticed. Describe an experiment rather than awarding yourself a mastery score. Keep the purpose in view: greater freedom to feel without suppression.

prompts: Which manageable feeling did I choose, and what helped invite it?
What sensations and images accompanied it?
What helped me return toward neutral?
Did I feel more able to be present, or was I trying to cover something up?
What scale would be appropriate for another attempt?

obstacles.title: I cannot detach from an unpleasant feeling
obstacles.response: The questions sheet says to stop that part and use pleasant emotions for now. Revisit earlier releasing-emotions and inventory work rather than intensifying the session.

obstacles.title: I get tired quickly
obstacles.response: The obstacles sheet expects fatigue and recommends rest before another repetition. More intensity or more repetitions are not required to prove progress.

obstacles.title: I am afraid of becoming overwhelmed
obstacles.response: The course recommends slowing down, choosing smaller non-overwhelming emotions, and increasing only as comfort develops. Skipping a difficult feeling is allowed.

obstacles.title: I use the practice to avoid sadness or anger
obstacles.response: The practice guide explicitly warns against covering unpleasant feelings with gratitude. Its stated aim is freedom to feel, not emotional suppression.

stories.title: The child on the manhole cover
stories.summary: Gary recounts an inner experience during an intensive retreat. In his imagery, a manhole cover held down a powerful flow of life, and a young version of himself stood on it. The child supplied clever reasons not to remove the cover: feeling fully might lead to pain or loss of control. Gary found that arguing with this character did not resolve the conflict. In his account, he changed approach, embraced the frightened child, and experienced the cover lifting along with intense emotion. This is his description of a personal meditative image, not a literal event or a required visualization for the weekly assignment.
stories.lesson: The story illustrates meeting fear of feeling with acceptance rather than relying only on argument.

stories.title: The imagined conversation inside the car
stories.summary: In You Are Dreaming, Gary invites listeners sitting in a room to imagine being in a car while rehearsing an argument with someone elsewhere. The listener can notice several layers at once: the present room, the imagined car, and the further imagined conversation. The example makes his use of dreaming concrete: he is describing the mind's ability to create a compelling scene, dialogue, and emotion. Becoming aware of those layers can make the emotional story easier to recognize as an activity of imagination. The illustration is not a claim that ordinary reality is unreal or that every concern should be dismissed.
stories.lesson: Notice the difference between a present event and an emotional scene being rehearsed in imagination.

storiesNote: The manhole cover is a personal meditative account; the nested conversation is a teaching example. Neither is evidence for a general psychological mechanism.

cheatsheet.principle: Practice a more flexible relationship with feeling, including the ability to release and rest.
remember: Begin with pleasant, manageable emotions.
Return to breath and present sensation after releasing the image.
Skip unpleasant emotions if detaching is difficult.
Rest when tired; no repetition quota is assigned.
Do not use positivity to suppress a feeling already present.
Freedom to feel matters more than speed.
cheatsheet.try: Invite a small feeling of gratitude, notice it, then release the image and return to neutral.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Treating intense emotion, instant control, or permanent happiness as a test of worth.
cheatsheet.question: Am I becoming more willing to feel, or more skilled at avoiding a feeling?

quiz.question: What should you do if an unpleasant emotion becomes hard to detach from?
options: Increase its intensity until you win
Stop that part and use pleasant emotions for now
Keep going because discomfort always proves progress
quiz.explanation: This is explicit guidance in the week's Common Questions.

quiz.question: Which use of gratitude does the practice guide warn against?
options: Enjoying appreciation during a chosen practice
Returning to gratitude after a rest
Using it to cover and suppress an unpleasant emotion
quiz.explanation: The stated goal is greater freedom to feel all emotions, not a new method of avoidance.

quiz.question: What is the larger benefit emphasized by the course?
options: More comfort and presence with feeling
Never feeling sadness again
Creating every emotion in two seconds this week
quiz.explanation: The questions place more emphasis on presence and releasing than on achieving a dramatic speed.

reflection: What changed in my confidence about feeling and letting go?
What sign told me to rest or reduce the scale?
Where might greater comfort with emotion support a choice I have been avoiding?
coverageNote: The lesson and written safeguards are combined here because the audio's intensity language needs the questions sheet's smaller-scale and stop-if-stuck guidance. Free of the Ego and You Are Dreaming extend the course's spiritual language about identity and imagination. Physiological and metaphysical explanations remain attributed course claims.

title: What You Want
overview: After questioning inherited ideals and perfection demands, you may be less certain what you actually want. This week treats that uncertainty as a workable starting point. Gary asks you to write what you do not want, use those details to discover what you do want, and explore different areas of life with particular attention to their emotional quality. The focus is how you want to express yourself and participate, not only what you want to possess or look like. The lesson also investigates shame about desire, fear of disappointment, and pressure to design an entire life perfectly. A revisable practice life makes the task smaller and more realistic.
outcomes: Create a specific don't-want and do-want inventory across chosen areas of life.
Distinguish an enjoyable expression or interaction from a borrowed image of success.
Identify resistance to desire and choose a manageable, revisable direction.

concepts.title: Begin sideways: what you do not want
concepts.explanation: When a blank page about your ideal life feels impossible, the lesson suggests beginning with concrete experiences you do not want. You may know that you do not want disrespectful interactions, chronic boredom, or work that consumes every evening. Writing makes the information more specific than a vague feeling of dissatisfaction. From there, ask what quality would be preferable. The opposite is a starting clue, not automatically a complete answer. Less boredom might mean creativity, outdoor activity, collaboration, or a new challenge. Investigate the actual experience you want rather than settling for a slogan.

concepts.title: Describe expression and emotional quality
concepts.explanation: Gary asks what you want to be doing and expressing, not only which title, partner, house, or income you want to have. Look back at moments you enjoyed in a job or relationship: solving a problem, listening closely, making something, learning, joking, or helping somebody succeed. Then ask what environment supports those expressions. Emotional qualities such as respect, ease, challenge, playfulness, and connection make the description more useful. You can later compare possible jobs or arrangements with that profile, instead of forcing yourself into an attractive label that does not fit daily experience.

concepts.title: Desire need not equal selfishness
concepts.explanation: The lesson describes how earlier messages about sharing, behaving, or being responsible can become a blanket rule against wanting anything for yourself. Gary distinguishes honoring a desire from being unkind or taking from others. The supporting article validates needs for rest, creativity, connection, affection, and one's own voice, while keeping other people's freedom of choice. Notice the difference between a request and a demand. Generosity toward yourself can coexist with consideration for others. The inventory asks what the label selfish is doing in a particular situation rather than declaring every impulse wise.

concepts.title: Fear of disappointment can hide desire
concepts.explanation: One obstacle is the belief that not wanting will protect you from loss or failure. Gary describes an inner strategy that avoids desire because a hoped-for result might be taken away or might never arrive. The side exploration summarizes a related chain: do not try, then you cannot fail, then the Judge has less material to attack. The exercise invites you to notice this strategy and inventory its stories. Wanting something, pursuing it, and responding to a disappointing outcome are related but distinct processes. You can examine the feared consequence without requiring yourself to want more immediately.

concepts.title: A practice life can be revised
concepts.explanation: Trying to define the next several decades can turn a useful inquiry into a perfection test. The lesson proposes a practice life: choose a manageable direction for a period, learn through participation, and review it as you change. If even that feels too large, the questions suggest starting with today, this week, or dinner. Your future self will have information and opportunities you do not have now. The plan can acknowledge that uncertainty instead of pretending to solve it. This week mainly clarifies desire and resistance; the following lesson develops motivation and action more fully.

visual.title: From dissatisfaction to a living direction
visual.intro: A study illustration of the course's iterative approach to discovering what you want.

steps.label: Notice the unwanted
steps.detail: Describe a concrete experience or interaction that does not work for you.

steps.label: Find the desired quality
steps.detail: Name what you would prefer to do, express, and feel.

steps.label: Make it realistic
steps.detail: Include ordinary difficulties, trade-offs, and other people's choices.

steps.label: Choose a small horizon
steps.detail: Design the next version rather than the whole lifetime.

steps.label: Review and revise
steps.detail: Let experience improve the plan.

visual.takeaway: The list is a working direction, not a permanent contract with your future.

practice.title: Write what you do and do not want
practice.cadence: The assignment asks you to listen and write across areas of life. The lesson says the process can take weeks or months and be revisited periodically; no fixed daily duration is assigned.

steps.title: Choose one area first
steps.body: Select relationships, work, home, finances, spiritual life, or emotional life. Beginning with one area is a manageable way to use the course's broader list.

steps.title: Write what you do not want
steps.body: Use specific experiences rather than only labels. Describe the interaction, activity, or emotional quality that does not work for you.

steps.title: Explore the wanted experience
steps.body: Write what you would like instead. Ask how you want to act and express yourself, what daily interactions would be like, and how you want to feel while participating.

steps.title: Add realistic detail
steps.body: Include how differences or setbacks would be handled. In a relationship, for example, describe respectful disagreement rather than assuming there will never be conflict. In a financial plan, include a practical route rather than relying on a windfall.

steps.title: Inventory the resistance
steps.body: Notice shame, unworthiness, fear of loss, the label selfish, or pressure to get everything perfect. Write these as character statements for investigation, not commands that automatically settle the decision.

steps.title: Choose a revisable direction
steps.body: Make the horizon small enough to work with. You can start with today or this week, or choose a longer practice-life project. Name a first possible action and a time to reconsider what you have learned.

steps.title: Honor a manageable desire
steps.body: The questions suggest acting on a small appropriate desire when possible, or at least appreciating the feeling when you choose not to act. Let the response be thoughtful rather than an obligation to satisfy every impulse.

prompts: In this area, what do I specifically not want?
How do I want to express myself and feel instead?
What would a normal difficult day look like in the life I want?
What story appears when I allow myself to want this?
What is the next version I can try, and when will I review it?

obstacles.title: I have no idea what I want
obstacles.response: The questions say to make the question smaller: today, this week, or a meal. The lesson also recommends mining enjoyable moments in previous experiences.

obstacles.title: Wanting something feels selfish or unsafe
obstacles.response: Inventory the exact belief. The supporting article distinguishes honoring needs and making respectful requests from demanding that others provide everything.

obstacles.title: I must design my whole life correctly
obstacles.response: Use the practice-life approach. You have permission to learn, change, and rewrite your direction as new possibilities become visible.

obstacles.title: Imagining happiness brings up shame
obstacles.response: The obstacles sheet treats this as a chance to identify a belief that has opposed your desire. Reduce the scope and write the character's words without treating them as the final truth.

stories.title: The perfect partner list without conflict
stories.summary: A client showed Gary a list of what he wanted in a partner, similar to a dating profile. Gary asked how he wanted the relationship to handle conflict. The client paused: his picture had not included any. The example moves the inquiry from an idealized person to the texture of a real relationship. Even people who care about one another have different preferences and occasional reactions. A more useful list includes listening, respect, negotiation, responsibility for one's projections, and the way disagreements are repaired. The point is not to lower every hope, but to include the daily processes that make a relationship workable.
stories.lesson: Describe how life works when differences arise, not only how it looks in a fantasy.

stories.title: From Navy engineering to consultative sales
stories.summary: Gary explains that he enjoyed solving engineering problems in the Navy: tracing systems of pumps, valves, and other equipment to find what was wrong. He did not enjoy owning every urgent problem while working with very little sleep. Later he also noticed that he wanted to serve people, but a corporate management role did not support the way he wanted to help. By separating those desired expressions from job titles, he eventually found outside consultative sales involving pumps and valves. He could troubleshoot a customer's problem and provide useful service in an environment that supported that effort. He calls this one of his practice lives, not his final identity.
stories.lesson: Look for the expressions and working conditions you enjoy before choosing a role to fit them.

storiesNote: These are paraphrases of the course's client example and Gary's career account.

cheatsheet.principle: Define a revisable life direction through the ways you want to act, relate, and feel.
remember: Start with what you do not want if desire is unclear.
Describe emotional quality, not only objects or status.
Include conflict, constraints, and practical paths.
Watch the labels selfish and not deserving.
A practice life can change as you learn.
You can start with one day or one small desire.
cheatsheet.try: Complete: I enjoy expressing __, especially in an environment where __.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Letting the Judge or an idealized success image write the whole list.
cheatsheet.question: What would I enjoy doing in this life, rather than merely being seen to have?

quiz.question: What is the recommended starting point when what you want feels unclear?
options: Write specific things you do not want, then explore preferred qualities.
Choose the most impressive goal you can imagine.
Wait until you know your entire future.
quiz.explanation: The lesson uses the don't-want list as a practical entry into clearer desire.

quiz.question: What is a practice life?
options: A fantasy with no real actions
A manageable direction you can learn from and revise
A plan that must never change
quiz.explanation: The concept reduces perfection pressure and leaves room for growth and new information.

quiz.question: Which relationship detail best reflects the written assignment?
options: We never disagree about anything.
My partner always knows what I need.
We listen respectfully and negotiate when our preferences differ.
quiz.explanation: The client anecdote asks learners to include realistic ways of handling conflict and differences.

reflection: Which desired quality felt like my own rather than a borrowed standard?
What resistance became visible when I imagined having it?
What is small enough to try before I revise the list?
coverageNote: Includes the practice, obstacles, questions, written lesson, Help Asking For What You Want, the Side Explorations handout, and We've let go of desire. The study prompts are optional scaffolding for the actual written assignment, not extra course requirements.

title: Build a New Dream
overview: This week brings the previous skills together around the life direction you described in What You Want. Gary teaches two practices: imagining the desired life with gratitude and confidence, and bringing attention into the body to connect intention with action. Earlier skepticism helped dismantle limiting beliefs; now the lesson asks you to notice when habitual disbelief also undermines a chosen new direction. The crucial distinction is that imagining is not enough. The written lesson repeatedly connects belief with action, skill, learning, and real-world conditions. This is an experiment in motivation and participation, not a promise that the world will deliver everything you visualize.
outcomes: Use a specific desired direction as material for gratitude and confidence practice.
Connect a bodily sense of intention with one concrete action.
Distinguish encouragement to act from a guarantee that imagination controls external events.

concepts.title: A different tool for a different phase
concepts.explanation: Earlier work asks you to question stories and detach from limiting identities. Gary compares that work to dismantling an old house. Building a new dream calls for a different use of attention: choose a direction and give it enough confidence and participation to develop. The obstacles sheet warns that a well-practiced Skeptic can begin dismissing every new possibility automatically. Notice that habit without abandoning practical discernment. You can suspend an untested verdict that you cannot do something while still checking costs, skills, conditions, and results. Supportive belief and real-world feedback have different jobs.

concepts.title: Desire, confidence, and action belong together
concepts.explanation: The lesson builds from the emotional quality of your What You Want list. Desire supplies a reason to participate; faith is Gary's term for confidence in a possibility; will is his term for the embodied force of acting. He explicitly says that belief by itself is insufficient. It can make an action feel possible, but the action still has to be taken and skills may need to be learned. A useful study version of this framework asks three questions: what matters to me, what would support willingness, and what can I actually do next?

concepts.title: Imagine the result and the learning path
concepts.explanation: The gratitude practice places you imaginatively in a future where a desired way of life is present. The important detail is that you also look back on the actions that helped create it, including attempts that did not work and what you learned from them. This keeps the picture connected to a process rather than only a finished reward. The practice guide recommends working on smaller areas separately when the whole list is too much. Focus on how you want to express yourself and interact. The image is motivational rehearsal, not evidence that the outcome has already occurred.

concepts.title: Use the body to begin
concepts.explanation: The second practice shifts attention from repeated deliberation into movement. Gary describes a standing exercise influenced by martial arts: feel the lower center of the body, breathe naturally, shift weight, and notice movement from that center. He calls this connecting with will. A seated version is allowed in the lesson. The practical endpoint is doing something on your action list rather than perfecting a sensation or proving a theory about energy. If the feeling is subtle, the questions recommend earlier acceptance and silent-mind practices. No dramatic bodily experience is required before a small useful action.

concepts.title: Skill and conditions still matter
concepts.explanation: The written lesson directly says that the law of attraction is not like gravity and that other forces affect outcomes. It uses an investment example to show that confidence and effort can still be poorly timed or unskillful. The supporting wealth article adds a feedback loop: take an action, measure the result, and adjust the next action. It also asks whether you are trading happiness for what you gain. Treat the course's spiritual language as Gary's perspective while keeping this practical distinction: your participation can influence events, but it does not make you the only force in the world.

visual.title: A dream becomes a sequence of actions
visual.intro: A study illustration combining the course's desire, gratitude, will, and feedback practices.

steps.label: Choose a direction
steps.detail: Use one specific part of your What You Want list.

steps.label: Feel its value
steps.detail: Imagine the expression and invite gratitude for the possibility.

steps.label: Connect with willingness
steps.detail: Bring attention into the body and the next movement.

steps.label: Take a skilled step
steps.detail: Do one concrete action or learn a missing skill.

steps.label: Learn and adjust
steps.detail: Observe the result and refine the next step.

visual.takeaway: Confidence helps you act; feedback helps the action become more skillful.

practice.title: Gratitude for a new dream, then embodied action
practice.cadence: Practice the two exercises separately before combining them. The lesson suggests nurturing the gratitude/confidence state for 20–30 minutes periodically, but the written summary sets no mandatory daily quota. Smaller parts of the desired-life list can be practiced separately.

steps.title: Choose one part of your list
steps.body: Select a relationship quality, activity, work direction, or another manageable aspiration from Week 23. Identify a concrete action that would help explore or develop it.

steps.title: Begin with present gratitude
steps.body: In a quiet place, bring attention to breathing and something you appreciate now. Let this be an actual feeling to explore rather than a statement you are required to believe.

steps.title: Imagine the desired expression
steps.body: Picture a future in which this part of life is present. Notice how you participate, relate, and express yourself. Invite gratitude for the experience, remembering that this is imagination.

steps.title: Include the imperfect route
steps.body: Imagine looking back on the small steps, learning, persistence, and adjustments that contributed. Include actions that did not work as expected and the information they gave you.

steps.title: Explore the body-centered exercise
steps.body: As described in the lesson, stand with a comfortable stable stance and soft knees, or use the permitted seated version. Attend to the lower center of the body, breathe normally, and gently notice how weight shifts and movement begin. Adapt or omit movement that does not suit you.

steps.title: Direct attention into one action
steps.body: Choose a safe, practical step from your list and do it: make an inquiry, practice a skill, draft something, or complete a useful errand. The step, not an intense sensation, is the bridge into daily life.

steps.title: Record the result and refine
steps.body: Write what you did, what happened, and what you learned. As the supporting article suggests, adjust the next action. Keep appreciation and willingness separate from a promise about results.

prompts: What specific way of expressing myself am I building?
What small actions might contribute, including learning I still need?
What did gratitude or bodily attention change about my willingness?
What action did I actually take?
What result or information will shape my next step?

obstacles.title: The Skeptic dismisses every possibility
obstacles.response: The obstacles sheet asks you to notice habitual disbelief applied to the new dream. Let a possibility receive an honest experiment while retaining practical checks and feedback.

obstacles.title: Responsibility feels like an invitation to blame
obstacles.response: The course suggests inventorying the fear and the character story that equates responsibility with punishment. Make the action smaller rather than turning the project into a test of your worth.

obstacles.title: I cannot feel my will
obstacles.response: The questions describe this as something that may develop with practice and point back to acceptance, silent mind, and releasing emotions. A subtle or absent special sensation does not prevent an ordinary action.

obstacles.title: I believed in it, so why did it not happen?
obstacles.response: The lesson says belief alone does not determine outcomes. Consider skill, timing, conditions, and other people's actions; use the result to learn rather than condemn yourself.

stories.title: Harry Potter sees that the spell is possible
stories.summary: Gary uses a scene from a Harry Potter film as a storybook illustration of confidence. Harry had thought his father cast the spell that saved him from the Dementors. After returning to the scene through time travel, he realizes he is the one who must cast it. Having already witnessed the result helps him believe he can act. Gary connects that fictional sequence with the exercise of imagining a desired future before taking steps toward it. He immediately distinguishes the illustration from passive wishing: believing in a possibility is useful because it can inspire action, not because a thought alone guarantees a result.
stories.lesson: An image of possibility can support willingness to act; it is not a substitute for the action.

stories.title: Learning to build the website
stories.summary: Gary describes deciding to create his own website. Once he had chosen the direction, the next step was to learn the necessary tool. He went to a bookstore, worked through a tutorial, opened the relevant program, and completed its practice exercises. He uses this ordinary sequence to distinguish endless contemplation from using the mind in service of an action. The learning was not bypassed by confidence; it was part of carrying the intention into the world. This makes a useful counterweight to the lesson's language of manifesting: a new project may require a book, repeated practice, and unfamiliar skills.
stories.lesson: Let the mind help execute and learn, instead of only reconsidering whether to begin.

storiesNote: The Harry Potter example is explicitly fictional. The website account is Gary's own illustration of learning through action.

Other forces and conditions still affect outcomes.
Measure, adjust, and notice whether the pursuit serves the life you want.

cheatsheet.watchFor: Turning confidence into certainty that the world must deliver a result.
